extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and other scientists asked to review journal articles in ecology and evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting peer review of journal manuscripts in ecology and evolution, covering whether to accept invitations, how to prepare and structure reports, section-by-section checklists, post-review duties, and ethical responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation — questions to consider before accepting
rubrics_metrics.description: When invited to review an article there are a few key questions to consider before accepting the invitation: Does the subject area of the article match my expertise? Do I have time to review within the timescale requested by the journal? Do I have any conflicts of interest that might prohibit me from reviewing the article objectively? Do I actually want to review this article?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journals ask for articles to be reviewed within 2–3 weeks (some shorter). If any reasons to decline exist, respond straight away. It is OK to say no; better than replying late or submitting a low-quality review. If you accept, commit the time needed and inform the editorial office promptly if you cannot meet the deadline or must withdraw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic principles of reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Always treat the paper with the utmost confidentiality; take an objective, independent approach; be attentive as your report will influence decisions; your role is to improve the science; provide evidence for statements; use simple language so authors (including non-native English speakers) can understand; conduct reviews professionally, courteously, collegially and politely; never contact the authors directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put aside subjective feelings about topic/authors, recognize the influence of the report on careers and journals, and balance critical scrutiny with constructive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation — how to get started
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have not reviewed for a particular journal before, read the aims and scope and consult the reviewer guidelines. Also look at the reviewer form to find out which questions you are expected to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before detailed appraisal read the article from start to finish to get an overview. The majority of your report will be free-text comments to authors and confidential comments to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview comments checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the article ask: Is there a clear and valid motivation for the study? Is the research question/hypothesis/prediction clearly presented? Does the research follow logically from prior knowledge and have potential to advance the field? Is the article appropriately structured and clearly presented? Can you summarise the key message? Does the title reflect the contents and is it engaging? Does the article fit the journal scope? Does it take account of relevant literature? Is there significant overlap with previous publications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your answers to these questions should form the opening comments in your report — succinctly summarise major strengths and weaknesses and the paper’s key message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section-by-section assessment — general approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a methodical approach by appraising each common section in turn (abstract/summary, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion). Provide evidence for statements whether positive or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most articles use standard headings; comment on each relevant section and be specific about where evidence supports your judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary/abstract checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it concisely written? Does it provide a clear overview of the work? Does it contain the essential facts from the paper? Does the final point place the work in a broader context, highlighting its significance?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag missing essential facts or lack of context; comment on whether the abstract accurately reflects the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this provide a clear, concise background to the study? Does it enable understanding of the aims and hypotheses? Have the authors elaborated sufficiently on the context? Has the motivation been adequately explained? Is there satisfactory citation of prior literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for clear framing of research questions and appropriate referencing of prior work; point out missing background or unclear motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the methodology sound? Have procedures been sufficiently described? Is there enough detail for replication? Is it clear what was recorded and which units were used? Are the statistical design and analyses appropriate? Have important details been left out? Where appropriate, has ethical approval been obtained?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about methodological flaws or omissions; suggest corrections or additional information needed for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results provided in a form that is easy to interpret and understand? Have results for all the questions asked been provided? Are the data of sufficient quality and quantity? Are figures and tables appropriate? Have the correct units been used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out unclear or missing results, inappropriate presentation, or insufficient data to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion and conclusions checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors answered their research question(s)/hypotheses? Are the conclusions drawn from the results justified? Has the significance of the study been fully explained? By how much has this study advanced current understanding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether claims overreach data, recommend tempering conclusions where appropriate, and assess contribution to the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary points on reviewer behaviour and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Be objective; include details of what is good about the article and highlight problems; look for novelty and importance; recognise that no study is perfect; be constructive; be thorough and thoughtful; evaluate both idea quality and experimental details/results; be specific and factually accurate; recognise opinion versus fact; be civil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles should guide the tone and content of both comments to authors and confidential comments to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-review responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible agree to review revisions/resubmissions you previously reviewed to provide consistency. Do not include anything that appears to be a decision about the paper in comments to authors (the decision is made by editors). As a courtesy, journals often copy other reviewers’ comments to you. The journal will never reveal your identity to authors without your permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use other reviewers’ reports to learn and spot missed issues; if identity is revealed (signed review) and disputes arise, advise authors to contact the editorial office rather than entering direct discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals — guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can request reconsideration of a rejection. Appeals are often handled by the editor and associate editor; in rare cases technical details may prompt the editor to approach reviewers for further comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you feel an editorial decision is wrong because a fatal flaw was overlooked, contact the editorial office so the decision can be revisited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality (ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: You are bound to confidentiality about the work you review. You must not take ideas presented and pass them as your own and must not disclose unpublished data. It is acceptable to ask a colleague for advice as long as authors’ names are not revealed and unnecessary details remain confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek journal permission before involving others; maintain confidentiality throughout; do not use or disclose material prior to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness and management of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion should be based solely on the presented work and not on prejudices. Be sensitive to gender bias, geographical bias, seniority bias, and confirmation bias and check whether your opinion may have been influenced by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate in assessing whether subjective biases affect judgments; be particularly mindful regardless of the peer review model used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and research ethics — duty to report concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviewers should take responsibility for reporting concerns regarding unethical practice (fabricated data, falsified data, stealing data, animal welfare breaches, duplicate/multiple submission and publication, unjustified or ghost authorship, conflicts of interest). Notify the editorial office if you suspect a breach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most journals have procedures to investigate concerns without revealing your identity; give examples of misconduct (definitions provided) and let the editorial office handle investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate/multiple submission and duplicate publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting an article to various journals concurrently or submitting over-lapping material to different journals is problematic. Duplicate publication may result when more than one journal accepts/publishes the same or substantially similar article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If suspected, notify editorial office; editors need to know if material is under consideration elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship is usually granted to those who have substantially contributed. Unjustified authorship (gift/honorary) is assignment to people who have not made substantial contributions. Ghost authorship is omission of those who have substantially contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag suspect authorship practices to the editorial office; authorship should meet standard contribution criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (for reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest that prevent impartial evaluation should be declared and will usually preclude reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, disclose to the editorial office and they will advise; do not review if you cannot be impartial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data archiving — reviewer expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals recommend or mandate that data associated with an article be archived in a public repository. Depositing data is usually required once a decision about publication is made; reviewers normally will not have access to archived data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewing the archived data is not generally part of reviewer duties unless stated (e.g., Molecular Ecology). If data are available you may inspect them, and you may suggest authors archive additional data or move material into supplementary files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling supporting information and supplementary files
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporting information or supplementary files are usually provided at submission but most journals do not expect them to be reviewed. They are not part of the published version of record but are usually posted online with the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may consult supplementary material for clarity, suggest moving information between main text and support files, or request additional supporting information if needed to assess conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access vs subscription journal reviewing criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Some open access journals (e.g. PLOS ONE) require reviewers to comment only on scientific and ethical integrity and clarity, not on importance or novelty; other OA journals (PLOS Biology, eLife) are selective and expect judgment on importance. Familiarise yourself with journal-specific guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the standards appropriate to the journal’s editorial criteria and aims and scope when judging manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying different standards across journals
rubrics_metrics.description: While your main role is to judge the science, you should keep in mind a journal’s aims/scope and the quality of articles expected. Case studies or niche pieces may be acceptable in one journal but not another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether and why you would expect an article to appear in the specific journal and support your opinion with reasons in comments to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential comments to editor vs comments to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential comments to editors should not significantly differ in overall message from comments to authors. The overall message of both should be the same; statements about whether an article should be published should be made only to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the confidential channel to summarise judgement and advise editors on procedural or sensitive issues, but avoid contradicting the comments visible to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewing, passing reviews to students or reviewing with supervisor
rubrics_metrics.description: You may suggest a student as an alternative reviewer or use review as a mentoring opportunity by involving a student under your supervision, but it is crucial to inform the journal in advance and seek consent. Include the student’s name so they get credit; if the student does most of the work, the review could be submitted under their own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully check any co-review before submission; when reviewing with a supervisor is used as training, ensure transparency with the journal so credit and confidentiality are handled correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asking colleagues for advice on aspects of a review
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to ask a colleague for advice (e.g. statistical analyses) provided you do not disclose authors’ names and keep unnecessary article details confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform the journal if you involve others and follow their policy; maintain confidentiality and do not reveal identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to spend on a review (guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: How long reviewing takes varies, but a BMJ reviewer survey found review quality increased with time up to 3 hours but not beyond; it is advisable to set aside 3–5 hours for the task depending on article type and length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an article is of such poor quality that it does not justify detailed review, indicate this but do not spend excessive time correcting basic problems; be more lenient with inexperienced authors or non-native English speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and copyediting expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are significant language problems, flag this in your comments so authors can be asked to improve language. You could edit a paragraph or two to highlight the kind of mistakes, but you should not feel it necessary to copyedit the manuscript yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish substantive scientific issues from language/formatting; suggest professional language help if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should peer review? — qualifications and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be carried out by those suitably 'qualified' — expertise can come from years of academic experience, in-depth PhD study, or practical field experience. Editors often select reviewers who have recently published on related subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are unsure of your suitability, consider your topical expertise and recent publications; volunteer or accept only when you have appropriate expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Three traditional peer review types: single-blind (authors do not know reviewers), double-blind (authors and reviewers hidden), open peer review (identities known).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the model the journal uses as it affects confidentiality and disclosure expectations; examples of journals using each model are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with alternative peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Other forms include cascading peer review (declined articles referred to another journal with reviewer comments), third-party peer review services (independent organisations arrange review), post-publication peer review platforms, and preprint servers which provide early feedback but not formal peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know how these models affect the review process, whether reviewer comments might be forwarded, and whether preprints or post-publication comments are relevant to your evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor decision factors and roles of editorial staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors make final decisions guided by: aims and scope, associate editor recommendation, reviewer comments, other recently published articles, journal priorities, and page budgets. Associate editors make initial expert assessment, select appropriate reviewers, scrutinize reviewers’ comments, provide their own assessment and recommendations. The editorial office checks files, provides central contact, and ensures in-house style and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame your review to provide evidence and clear recommendations that help associate editors and editors make balanced decisions; understand editors consider multiple factors beyond scientific soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibilities (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are subject area experts asked to: provide a detailed, objective report on merits; identify flaws in design/analysis/interpretation; highlight ethical concerns; comment on appropriateness of cited literature; and offer a view on suitability for publication in the target journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on scientific soundness, clarity, completeness, and ethical integrity; provide constructive suggestions and evidence for criticisms.
